title: WHY DID JESUS GO BACK TO ADAM AND EVE WHEN THEY ASKED HIM ABOUT DIVORCE?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS GO BACK TO ADAM AND EVE WHEN THEY ASKED HIM ABOUT DIVORCE?

They wanted to know how a marriage could end. Jesus took them back to the moment marriage began. And what He revealed was bigger than divorce—it exposed the human heart, the tragedy of broken promises, and the breathtaking grace of a Savior who came to redeem what sin had shattered.
There is something deeply unsettling about the way Jesus answered this question.
The Pharisees came to Him asking about divorce.
But Jesus started talking about Adam and Eve.
Not Moses.
Not divorce certificates.
Not the legal arguments that had divided religious teachers for generations.
Adam. And Eve.

A man and a woman standing at the beginning of human history, before betrayal had poisoned trust, before shame had entered the human heart, before the first marriage had ever experienced the devastating consequences of sin.
Why?
Why would Jesus reach all the way back to the Garden of Eden when the question was about ending a marriage?
Because sometimes the most revealing thing about a question is not what someone asks.
It is what they have already decided to accept.
And the Pharisees were asking about the circumstances under which a marriage could be dissolved.
Jesus was about to remind them why marriage existed in the first place.
But there is another reason this conversation matters.
Somewhere reading this is a husband who knows he has failed his wife.
A wife who has cried herself to sleep beside someone who no longer seems to know her.
Someone divorced who still carries the weight of a promise that did not survive.
Someone who stayed in a marriage but feels emotionally abandoned.
Someone who was betrayed.
Someone who did the betraying.
Someone who has been told that their broken marriage means their life is permanently disqualified from God's purposes.
And someone who desperately needs to know whether the Jesus who defended God's design for marriage still has room in His heart for people whose marriages have fallen apart.
Stay with this.
Because the same Jesus who spoke uncompromisingly about the sacredness of marriage also came to save sinners.
And if we misunderstand either truth, we will misunderstand His heart.
Matthew 19:3 tells us that the Pharisees approached Jesus to test Him.
They asked:
“Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?”
— Matthew 19:3, King James Version
That phrase, for every cause, is important.
The question was not simply whether divorce existed under the Law of Moses.
It concerned the grounds on which a husband might divorce his wife.
Deuteronomy 24:1 had become the subject of serious disagreement among Jewish teachers. Some interpreted its language more restrictively, while others permitted divorce for a wider range of reasons.
The Pharisees were drawing Jesus into a disputed question.
And Matthew tells us their purpose was to test Him.
But Jesus refused to let the argument begin where they wanted it to begin.
Instead, He answered:
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?”
— Matthew 19:4–5, KJV
Then came the words that have echoed through Christian marriage ceremonies for centuries:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
— Matthew 19:6, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
Jesus did not begin by discussing how easily a marriage could be ended.
He began by declaring how seriously a marriage should be regarded.
And He grounded that seriousness in creation itself.
In the Greek text of Matthew 19:4, Jesus uses the expression:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς — ap’ archēs
It means from the beginning.
Not from the beginning of the Mosaic Law.
Not from the beginning of Israel's debates about divorce.
From the beginning.
Jesus was directing His listeners back to God's original intention.
Before the regulations addressing broken marriages, there was the creation of marriage.
Before the discussion about separation, there was a divine purpose for union.
And before human sin complicated everything, God had already shown that marriage was meant to be more than a disposable arrangement.
This is why Jesus returned to Genesis.
Not because He had forgotten the pain of broken relationships.
But because the existence of human brokenness does not erase the goodness of God's design.
Think about the world of Genesis 2.
Adam stands in the garden.
Creation is good.
The earth is filled with evidence of God's wisdom.
Yet the Lord declares something striking:
“It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.”
— Genesis 2:18, KJV
The Hebrew expression is:
עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ — ʿezer kenegdô
It describes a helper corresponding to him, someone suitable and complementary to him.
The word ʿezer does not imply inferiority. Elsewhere in Scripture, the same Hebrew noun is used of God as the help of His people.
Eve was not created as Adam's property.
She was not presented as an object to be discarded when life became inconvenient.
She was a fellow human being, bearing God's image, corresponding to him in a relationship of profound significance.
Genesis 2:23 records Adam's response:
“This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.”
It is the language of recognition.
Of kinship.
Of belonging.
And then Scripture declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
— Genesis 2:24, KJV
The Hebrew word translated cleave is:
דָּבַק — dabaq
It carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, or adhering closely.
The image is not of two strangers maintaining a convenient arrangement.
It is of a new and enduring bond.
And the phrase translated one flesh is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
One flesh.
A union involving embodied life, sexual intimacy, kinship, and a shared covenantal future.
Jesus takes this ancient declaration and gives it extraordinary weight.
God joins.
Human beings must not treat that joining lightly.
And suddenly the Pharisees' question looks different.
They were asking about permissible separation.
Jesus was speaking about sacred union.
They were examining the legal boundary.
Jesus was revealing the divine intention.
And that distinction still exposes something uncomfortable in us today.
Because human beings have an astonishing ability to ask the right religious questions while avoiding the deeper condition of their hearts.
We ask how much anger is acceptable before it becomes sin.
How far we can go before crossing a moral line.
How little forgiveness we can offer while still calling ourselves Christians.
How much selfishness a relationship can survive.
How many compromises we can justify.
And sometimes we ask what Scripture permits when what we really need to ask is what love requires.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus was not teaching that every struggling spouse should remain in danger.
He was not authorizing abuse.
He was not commanding a person to endure violence or coercion as proof of faithfulness.
God's design for marriage must never be twisted into a weapon against the vulnerable.
The Bible condemns violence, oppression, treachery, and cruelty. Christian teaching about covenant faithfulness cannot be separated from God's concern for justice and protection.

A person facing abuse may need immediate safety, separation, and appropriate legal or pastoral support. Questions about divorce and remarriage require careful attention to the whole counsel of Scripture, including Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:10–16, on which Christian traditions sometimes differ.
Jesus' words are sacred.
That is precisely why they must not be used carelessly.
Now notice what happens next.
The Pharisees do not simply accept His answer.
They press Him.
“Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away?”
— Matthew 19:7, KJV
And Jesus answers with one of the most devastating diagnoses of the human condition in the Gospels:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
— Matthew 19:8, KJV
There it is.
The problem beneath the argument.
Hardness of heart.
In the Greek text, Jesus speaks of:
σκληροκαρδία — sklērokardia
Hardheartedness.
A heart resistant to God's will.
A heart that has become stubborn, unyielding, or morally insensitive.
And this is where the passage becomes painfully personal.
Because hardness of heart does not always look like hatred.
Sometimes it looks like indifference.
Sometimes it sounds like, “I'm tired of trying.”
Sometimes it is refusing to apologize because pride feels safer than humility.
Sometimes it is treating a spouse's tears as an inconvenience.
Sometimes it is making promises before God and then quietly abandoning the responsibilities attached to them.
Sometimes it is refusing to seek help because admitting the truth would require change.
And sometimes it is using Bible verses to control another person while refusing to submit one's own behavior to the Lordship of Christ.
A heart can quote Scripture and still resist God.
A mouth can defend marriage while the life behind it dishonors the very covenant it claims to protect.
And a person can win an argument about divorce while losing the battle against selfishness.
That is the danger Jesus was exposing.
But do not misunderstand Him.
Not every divorce is proof that both spouses were equally hardhearted.
Not every abandoned person chose abandonment.
Not every betrayed spouse created the betrayal.
Not every marriage ends because both people refused to love.
Sin has victims as well as perpetrators.
Jesus knows the difference.
He sees what other people never saw.
He knows who tried.
Who lied.
Who prayed.
Who manipulated.
Who repented.
Who refused.
Who was afraid.
And who was left carrying consequences they never chose.
This is why we must never use Matthew 19 as a stone to throw at wounded people.
The passage is meant to bring us under the authority of Christ, not give us permission to sit in judgment over every broken family.
And yet Jesus' words still challenge us.
Because He does not allow the hardness of the human heart to redefine the goodness of God's original purpose.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
What a sentence.
It acknowledges that something has gone terribly wrong.
Marriage was created for faithful union.
But sin brought alienation.
Marriage was meant to reflect belonging.
But sin introduced blame.
Marriage was intended to be a place where two people could live in covenantal faithfulness.
But sin made betrayal possible.
And if you return to Genesis 3, you can almost hear the fracture.
God confronts Adam after the forbidden fruit has been eaten.
And Adam responds:
“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.”
— Genesis 3:12, KJV
The man who had once celebrated the woman as bone of his bones now speaks of her in the language of blame.
He does not deny eating.
But he points away from himself.
Toward the woman.
And indirectly toward the God who gave her.
Sin has entered the story.
And the relationship has changed.
The Bible does not explicitly say that Adam and Eve considered divorce. We should not invent that detail.
But it does show the devastating beginnings of shame, accusation, and fractured human relationships.
The very people joined together in the first marriage now experience the consequences of disobedience.
And here is the tragedy.
The problem was never merely that human beings needed better marriage rules.
The problem was that human beings needed redeemed hearts.
You can place two people in a beautiful ceremony.
You can surround them with flowers.
You can give them rings.
You can invite a pastor.
You can have them repeat vows while everyone cries.
But no ceremony can remove the sinful nature of the human heart.
A wedding can publicly establish a covenant.
It cannot, by itself, produce the holiness needed to honor that covenant.
That is why marriage needs more than romance.
It needs truth.
Repentance.
Faithfulness.
Patience.
Humility.
Forgiveness.
And the transforming grace of God.
But even here, there is something greater that Jesus wants us to see.
Because the One speaking in Matthew 19 is not merely a wise teacher explaining Genesis.
He is the eternal Son of God through whom all things were made.
John 1:3 declares:
“All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.”
And Colossians 1:16 teaches that all things were created through Christ and for Him.
Think about that.
The One explaining the beginning of marriage is the One through whom creation came into existence.
Jesus was not quoting Genesis as a detached observer.
He was speaking with the authority of the Creator.
And the Creator had entered a world filled with the wreckage of human sin.
He had come among people whose promises were broken.
Whose homes were fractured.
Whose hearts were hardened.
Whose shame was hidden behind religious appearances.
And He had not come merely to explain what was wrong.
He had come to redeem sinners.
That is where this story becomes more than a discussion about marriage.
It becomes a doorway into the Gospel.
Because the Bible uses the imagery of marriage to reveal something astonishing about Christ and His people.
In Ephesians 5, Paul calls husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Then, after speaking about the one-flesh union of husband and wife, he writes:
— Ephesians 5:32, KJV
Do you see the connection?
Human marriage is not the Gospel itself.
And no human spouse is a savior.
But marriage, rightly understood, can point beyond itself to the covenant love of Jesus Christ.
A love that gives.
A love that is faithful.
A love that is holy.
A love that does not exploit the beloved.
A love that sacrifices for the good of another.
And at the center of that picture stands Jesus.
Not demanding that sinners save themselves.
But giving Himself to save those who could never rescue themselves.
Here is the contrast that should humble every married person.
Jesus never sinned against His people.
Yet He bore the cost of their sin.
He was never unfaithful.
Yet He came to redeem the unfaithful.
He never broke His word.
Yet He died for people who had broken theirs.
He did not go to the cross because we had kept our promises perfectly.
He went because we had not.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired everything.
Not after we became impressive Christians.
Not after our reputations recovered.
Not after every consequence disappeared.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And suddenly the words from the beginning become even more profound.
Jesus takes us back to the beginning to show us what God intended.
But He does not leave us trapped in the ruins of what humanity destroyed.
He leads us toward the cross.
Where sin is confronted.
Where mercy is revealed.
Where forgiveness is purchased through His blood.
Where the guilty can repent.
Where the ashamed can come into the light.
Where a new life becomes possible.
This does not mean every broken marriage will be restored.
It does not mean repentance automatically rebuilds trust.
It does not mean reconciliation is always safe, possible, or required in the same form.
And it certainly does not mean forgiveness removes the need for accountability.
But it does mean that failure is not stronger than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
Your divorce may be part of your history.
It does not have to become the entirety of your identity.
Your betrayal may require confession, restitution, and difficult consequences.
But genuine repentance can still lead you toward the mercy of God.
Your marriage may be struggling.
But you do not have to keep feeding it with pride, dishonesty, and silence.
And if you are single, widowed, abandoned, or divorced, your worth is not measured by whether you are married.
Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Marriage is a good gift.
It is not the ultimate source of human salvation, dignity, or completeness.
The same Jesus who honored marriage also lived a fully holy human life without marrying.
And the apostle Paul affirmed the dignity and spiritual value of singleness in 1 Corinthians 7.
So no, Matthew 19 is not a declaration that married people are more valuable than unmarried people.
It is a declaration that God's gifts must be understood according to God's purposes.
And that includes marriage.
Perhaps the most difficult question is not why Jesus returned to Adam and Eve.
Perhaps it is why we are so tempted to avoid returning to God's original intention ourselves.
Because returning to the beginning forces us to confront the distance between what God intended and what we have sometimes accepted.
It asks the husband whether he is loving sacrificially or merely demanding respect.
It asks the wife whether she is pursuing truth and faithfulness rather than letting resentment silently govern her heart.
It asks both spouses whether they are treating each other as fellow image-bearers or as obstacles to personal happiness.
It asks the church whether it is protecting the vulnerable or merely protecting appearances.
It asks pastors whether they are preaching both covenant faithfulness and the Gospel of grace.
And it asks every believer whether we want Jesus to affirm our preferences or transform our hearts.
That last question is not limited to marriage.
It reaches into every part of life.
Because a hardened heart can ruin far more than a relationship.
It can resist conviction.
It can excuse sin.
It can weaponize religion.
It can reject correction.
It can refuse mercy.
It can become so accustomed to darkness that light begins to feel like an accusation.
And yet the Lord still calls sinners to repentance.
The promise of Ezekiel 36:26 speaks of God's power to give His people a new heart:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.”
What the hardened heart cannot accomplish by its own strength, God can begin to transform by His grace.
Not by pretending sin is harmless.
Not by denying the damage it causes.
But by bringing the sinner into the light of His holiness and mercy.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
And perhaps this is where you need to stop reading for a moment.
Not to examine your former spouse.
Not to rehearse everything another person did.
Not to gather another argument against someone who hurt you.
But to ask the Lord a question that requires courage.
“Jesus, is there something in my heart that I have refused to surrender?”
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe an affair no one knows about.
Maybe the way you speak to your spouse when nobody else is listening.
Maybe your refusal to apologize.
Maybe the shame you have carried for years because you believe God can forgive everyone except you.
Maybe you are not married at all, but you have been treating relationships as temporary arrangements rather than places where truth, dignity, and faithfulness matter.
Whatever it is, bring it to Christ.
Not because He is indifferent to sin.
But because He is the only Savior who can forgive sin and make us new.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to pretend before the One who already knows.
There is no need to defend the darkness before the One who calls us into the light.
And there is no need to confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work of conviction leads us toward the truth about sin and our need for Christ.
And in Christ, repentant sinners find mercy.
That is why this passage should leave us both trembling and hopeful.
Trembling because Jesus takes covenant faithfulness seriously.
Hopeful because the One who calls us to holiness is also the One who died for our sins and rose again.
The cross does not make marriage vows meaningless.
It teaches us how costly faithful love truly is.
Grace does not give us permission to continue in sin.
It calls us out of sin and into newness of life.
And repentance is not simply feeling terrible about what happened.
It is turning toward God in faith, acknowledging the truth, and beginning to walk in obedience through the power of His Spirit.
Some relationships may be healed through that process.
Others may remain broken because of choices that cannot be controlled by one person.
But a life surrendered to Christ is never beyond His power to transform.
And that is why I want you to remember something.
When Jesus returned to Adam and Eve, He was not trying to win a debate by appealing to nostalgia.
He was revealing the authority of God's design over human attempts to make covenant obligations disposable.
He was showing that the regulation of divorce in a fallen world was not the same thing as God's original purpose for marriage.
And in the larger story of Scripture, He was revealing our desperate need for the Redeemer who can change the human heart.
The Pharisees asked how a marriage could be dissolved.
Jesus reminded them what God had joined.
They appealed to what Moses had permitted.
Jesus exposed the hardness of the human heart.
And the Gospel reveals the Savior who came to deal with sin at its deepest root.
That is the journey.
From creation.
To corruption.
To the cross.
To the hope of new creation in Jesus Christ.
And it is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain religious curiosity for a few seconds before the next distraction.
Not to make people feel condemned without showing them the Savior.
But to keep bringing hearts back to Scripture, back to repentance, back to grace, and back to the Lord Jesus Christ.
If this message has challenged you, please do not let it disappear into your Facebook feed.
Not as a trophy of religious knowledge, but as something you can return to when your heart needs to remember what Jesus actually said.
And please, be part of the conversation.
You do not have to publish the details of your pain to be worthy of prayer.

If you have witnessed God's grace after failure, you are also welcome to share your testimony. Someone reading may need to know that repentance, healing, and a faithful new beginning are possible in Christ.
And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I invite you to do so.
Bring your spouse, your children, your friends, the struggling believer, the spiritually weary, and even the person who does not yet believe.
Let them encounter Scripture that does not hide the seriousness of sin or the greatness of God's mercy.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry is worth helping sustain.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical teaching, discipleship resources, and Christ-centered encouragement accessible to people who need them.
These resources are meant to help believers grow deeper in the Word, strengthen their understanding of Scripture, and continue following Jesus beyond a single article.
Scripture tells us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is the spirit in which I invite you.
Not through pressure.
Not through fear.
And never because salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual blessing can be purchased.
The Gospel is free because Jesus has already paid the price of our redemption.
But sharing biblical resources with more people still requires faithful stewardship, time, effort, and practical support.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can be reminders of truth, thoughtful gifts, and practical ways to help support the continued work.
A single public share may place this message before someone who would never have searched for it.
A thoughtful comment may encourage another believer to open up.
A saved article may become a timely reminder during a difficult season.
We cannot control how God will use every act of faithfulness.
But we can faithfully offer what we have.
And we can keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because this ministry is not ultimately about building an audience around a personality.
It is about helping people encounter the truth of the Gospel.
The truth that God created us with purpose.
That sin has damaged what He made good.
That His commandments reveal His holy character.
That Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
That repentance and faith are not empty religious words.
And that the grace of God does not merely cover our past—it begins to transform our future.
So before you leave, return with me to that moment in Matthew 19.
The Pharisees are standing before Jesus.
Their question is still hanging in the air.
They want to know when a man may send his wife away.
But Jesus takes them back to the beginning.
Back to the man and woman.
Back to the divine intention.
Back to the words one flesh.
Back to the sacred reality of what God joins together.
And perhaps the deepest question for us is no longer merely, “Why did Jesus return to Adam and Eve?”
Perhaps it is this:
What would change in our lives if we stopped asking how far we could move away from God's design and started asking how fully we could surrender to His will?
That question reaches the married and the unmarried.
The faithful and the fallen.
The betrayed and the repentant.
The wounded and the healing.
It reaches every person who has ever tried to justify what God is calling them to surrender.
And it brings us to the feet of Jesus.
Where truth is not negotiable.
Where sin is not excused.
Where the wounded are not forgotten.
And where mercy is still available to every sinner who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
Marriage began in a garden.
Human rebellion brought shame into the human story.
But redemption was accomplished through the crucified and risen Christ.
And one day, the people of God will rejoice at the marriage supper of the Lamb, when the final victory of Christ will be celebrated and His redeemed people will dwell with Him forever.
That is the greater hope toward which the whole story points.
Not that every earthly relationship will become perfect.
But that Jesus Christ will faithfully complete His work of redemption.
And until that day, we are called to trust Him.
To honor His Word.
To repent when we sin.
To protect those who are vulnerable.
To love with truth.
To forgive as He commands, without pretending that forgiveness erases justice or necessary boundaries.
And to remember that our deepest hope is not in a flawless human relationship.
It is in a faithful Savior.
The beginning reveals what sin shattered. The cross reveals how deeply God loves the people He came to redeem.
